lines.english: The horses said: "Listen, sheep, our hearts pain us when we see this: a man, the master, makes the wool of the sheep into a warm garment for himself. And the sheep has no wool."
Having heard this, the sheep fled into the plain.

versions.english:
The Sheep and the Horses

A sheep that had no wool saw horses, one of them pulling a heavy wagon, one carrying a big load, and one carrying a man quickly. The sheep said to the horses: "My heart pains me, seeing a man driving horses." The horses said: "Listen, sheep, our hearts pain us when we see this: a man, the master, makes the wool of the sheep into a warm garment for himself. And the sheep has no wool." Having heard this, the sheep fled into the plain.

versions.notes: Text copied programmatically from the HTML of the Archaeology magazine page (print view, Wayback snapshot http://web.archive.org/web/20130921200706id_/http://www.archaeology.org/exclusives/articles/1302-proto-indo-european-schleichers-fable?tmpl=component&print=1&layout=default&page=); the live URL now returns 404. Three snapshots (2013-09-21 normal view, 2013-09-21 print view, 2022-01-26 at /exclusives/articles/1302) give byte-identical text for both reconstructions. Earliest Wayback capture 2013-09-21; no publication date shown on the page. NOTATION: laryngeal indices and aspiration/labialization diacritics are HTML <sub>/<sup> markup in the source and are kept verbatim as literal <sub>…</sub>/<sup>…</sup> tags in source_form (e.g. h<sub>1</sub>, k<sup>w</sup>, d<sup>h</sup>); other tags (<b>, <i>, <strong>) were stripped and HTML entities unescaped. No Unicode normalization applied. source_form = published title + blank line + body paragraph; lines = title (line 1) + body split on sentence-final punctuation (not split at "!" inside the unclosed quotation after ḱlud<sup>h</sup>í). Quotes in the source are curly (“ ”); the quotation opened before ḱlud<sup>h</sup>í is never closed in the source. Sheep text uses <sup>h</sup>/<sup>w</sup>/<sup>wh</sup> throughout (no Unicode modifier letters). English is the article's translation of the fable (introduced as the translation of Schleicher's 1868 text, not a translation made for Byrd's version). Per-line english: lines 2-3 are null because the single English sentence "A sheep that had no wool saw horses, ..." spans both; line 5 joins two English sentences. Audio-only companions (not transcribed): SoundCloud player on the Archaeology page; https://www.as.uky.edu/sites/default/files/PIE%20-%20Sheep%20and%20Horses.mp3 (UK A&S podcast page https://www.as.uky.edu/podcasts/sheep-and-horses has no text).

H<sub>3</sub>rḗḱs dei̯u̯ós-k<sup>w</sup>e

H<sub>3</sub>rḗḱs h<sub>1</sub>est; só n̥putlós. H<sub>3</sub>rḗḱs súh<sub>x</sub>num u̯l̥nh<sub>1</sub>to. Tósi̯o ǵʰéu̯torm̥ prēḱst: "Súh<sub>x</sub>nus moi̯ ǵn̥h<sub>1</sub>i̯etōd!" Ǵʰéu̯tōr tom h<sub>3</sub>rḗǵm̥ u̯eu̯ked: "h<sub>1</sub>i̯áǵesu̯o dei̯u̯óm U̯érunom". Úpo h<sub>3</sub>rḗḱs dei̯u̯óm U̯érunom sesole nú dei̯u̯óm h<sub>1</sub>i̯aǵeto. "ḱludʰí moi, pter U̯erune!" Dei̯u̯ós U̯érunos diu̯és km̥tá gʷah<sub>2</sub>t. "Kʷíd u̯ēlh<sub>1</sub>si?" "Súh<sub>x</sub>num u̯ēlh<sub>1</sub>mi." "Tód h<sub>1</sub>estu", u̯éu̯ked leu̯kós dei̯u̯ós U̯érunos. Nu h<sub>3</sub>réḱs pótnih<sub>2</sub> súh<sub>x</sub>num ǵeǵonh<sub>1</sub>e.

versions.english:
The King and the God

Once there was a king. He was childless. The king wanted a son. He asked his priest: "May a son be born to me!" The priest said to the king: "Pray to the god Werunos." The king approached the god Werunos to pray now to the god. "Hear me, father Werunos!" The god Werunos came down from heaven. "What do you want?" "I want a son." "Let this be so," said the bright god Werunos. The king's lady bore a son.
versions.evidence_quote: Here, Andrew Byrd recites his version of the “The King and the God” in PIE, based on the work of linguists Eric Hamp and the late Subhadra Kumar Sen.

Three snapshots (2013-09-21 normal view, 2013-09-21 print view, 2022-01-26 at /exclusives/articles/1302) give byte-identical text for both reconstructions. Earliest Wayback capture 2013-09-21; no publication date shown on the page. NOTATION: laryngeal indices and aspiration/labialization diacritics are HTML / markup in the source and are kept verbatim as literal …/… tags in source_form (e.g. h1, kw, dh); other tags (, , ) were stripped and HTML entities unescaped. No Unicode normalization applied. source_form = published title + blank line + body paragraph; lines = title (line 1) + body split on sentence-final punctuation. The King and the God text mixes HTML markup (1, w in title) with Unicode modifier letters ʰ (U+02B0) and ʷ (U+02B7) (e.g. ǵʰéu̯torm̥, gʷah2t, Kʷíd); kept as published. Quotes are straight ("). A no-break space (U+00A0, from  ) between pótnih2 and súhxnum is kept. Title in source HTML was split across two elements (H3rḗḱs), joined after tag stripping. Line 2 english joins two English sentences ("Once there was a king. He was childless."). Second Byrd-affiliated publication of the same text: University of Kentucky College of Arts & Sciences Q&A "Fables of the Reconstruction: Andrew Byrd", https://linguistics.as.uky.edu/node/208112 (linked from UKNow as www.as.uky.edu/fables-reconstruction-andrew-byrd), introduced "This is what the fable, H3rḗḱs dei̯u̯ós-kwe (The King and the God), sounded like:". After collapsing its line-wrap whitespace it differs from the Archaeology text in 3 words: word 19: Archaeology 'dei̯u̯óm' vs UK 'de̯iu̯óm'; word 30: Archaeology 'moi,' vs UK 'moi̯,'; word 46: Archaeology 'dei̯u̯ós' vs UK 'de̯iu̯ós'. Audio-only companions (not transcribed): SoundCloud track 110083074 on the Archaeology page; https://www.as.uky.edu/sites/default/files/PIE%20-%20King%20and%20God.mp3 (podcast page https://stemcats.uky.edu/podcasts/king-and-god has no text).
